title: Dhul-Jalali wal-Ikram
tomorrow: what's fair when the one who wronged you is thirteen?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Malik al-Mulk, and a keyring resting in an open palm. The line: owner of all. Today, an apology at a coffee shop counter.
screen: `OWNER OF ALL.` → `AN APOLOGY AT THE COUNTER.`

segments.voice: A kid at a counter, hands jammed in his hoodie pocket, saying sorry to an adult while his mom waits by the door. Maybe you've stood on one side of a moment like that. Maybe both. Yesterday's question: when the apology finally comes, how do you take it without making the other person smaller? You can win the moment. You can also lose the person. The Qur'an has a two-part Name that holds exactly that balance.
screen: `SORRY, AT THE COUNTER.` → `WIN THE MOMENT, LOSE THE PERSON?` → `A TWO-PART NAME.`

segments.voice: In Surah ar-Rahman, after a long list of gifts, the verses turn: "Everyone that is thereon will pass away; There remaineth but the Countenance of thy Lord of Might and Glory." In Arabic, that title is Dhul-Jalali wal-Ikram. Jalal is majesty, greatness that doesn't need anyone's applause. Ikram is honoring, generosity, treating someone as worth something. Put together, it's a greatness that gives dignity instead of taking it. Nothing about that majesty requires anyone to be made small. Here's a line to tell a friend tonight. The Prophet, peace be upon him, used this Name in the words he said right after finishing a prayer: Allahumma antas-salam wa minkas-salam, tabarakta ya dhal-jalali wal-ikram. You are Peace, and from You is peace; blessed are You, Lord of Majesty and Generosity. And in another report, he told people to hold fast to ya dhal-jalali wal-ikram when they call on God. So back to the counter. Jalal says: you don't need to win this. Ikram says: honor him for coming. The two together might look like naming what happened plainly, thanking him for saying it, and pulling out a chair.
screen: `THERE REMAINETH BUT THE COUNTENANCE.` · `JALAL: MAJESTY. IKRAM: HONORING.` · `SAID RIGHT AFTER THE PRAYER.` · `YOU DON'T NEED TO WIN. HONOR HIM.` · then, large: `MAJESTY AND HONOR.`

segments.voice: Say the phrase slowly, out loud or under your breath: ya dhal-jalali wal-ikram, O Lord of Majesty and Generosity. Between each saying, bring to mind one person it would cost you something to honor this week. Let the phrase and that face sit side by side until the bell.
Dhul-Jalali wal-Ikram. Lord of Majesty and Generosity: great enough that no one needs to be made small.
Here's the line: majesty and honor, with room at the counter for both people. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: After prayer, Muslims say the Prophet's words: Allahumma antas-salam wa minkas-salam, tabarakta ya dhal-jalali wal-ikram.

fork.setup: a teammate who mocked you all season apologizes at practice, in front of everyone. what fits today's Name?
options: accept it plainly, thank them for saying it, and let them keep their dignity.
have them spell out every single thing they did, so it really counts.
laugh and say it never bothered you, so nobody feels awkward.
fork.reveal: jalal: you don't need to win. ikram: honor the one who came. the second option wins the moment; the third hides the truth.

original.note: Arabic: Lord of Majesty and Generosity, from Surah ar-Rahman.

trapdoor: what you thought: a grand royal title.
what it means: majesty joined to generosity, a greatness that honors others.
what a scholar hears: 55:27 and 55:78; the post-prayer words in Sahih Muslim 591; 'hold fast to ya dhal-jalali wal-ikram' in Jami' at-Tirmidhi.
guess: Lord of the Heavens and Earth

chat.says: Eli said sorry at the counter. i had a whole speech ready. dad just slid him a hot chocolate.
options: Dad did both: took it seriously and still honored Eli. Majesty and generosity.
Dad went too easy. Real dignity means Eli hears your full speech first.
Dad got it right: the hot chocolate means the wall doesn't matter now.
chat.meaning: Dhul-Jalali wal-Ikram joins majesty with honoring others. Taking an apology well can be serious and generous at once.
